speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure
that the house has been amused if not edified by the spectacle presented since this bill was first moved. We have a very amazing condition of affairs with respect to a matter that is regarded as of very serious importance to the Canadian people. The principle of the bill was approved of upon the second reading and the bill now stands for third reading, but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Euler) who was so intense in his statements of a year ago, has been so silent during the discussion of this bill that, in the language of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), that silence is impressive. We venture to direct attention to the fact that the government had taken rather a strange view in this matter. A year ago the government, speaking through its Minister of National Revenue, declared that the measure which has now been adopted by this house was impossible of realization. He made his declaration in language so vigorous and so strong that I think it would be unfair to the Canadian people to allow this measure to pass without directing attention to a few of the words he used on that occasion. On May 21, 1929, the hon. Minister of National Revenue, speaking on a motion which had been made in this house with respect to this very matter, namely, the export of liquor to the United States of America, used these words, as reported at page 2704 of Hansard of that year:
One of the arguments offered against our prohibiting the issuance of clearances is that the problem which the United States is now experiencing is one of their own making and that we are not primarily responsible. Another is-using the words of the man on the street- "let the United States enforce their own law." In the light of the statements which I made this afternoon, in connection with the lack of effort on the part of the United States to enforce their own law, I think that attitude is a very human and fairly reasonable one and that we might at least go slowly until we have some assurance and some evidence that they are trying to do for themselves what they are now asking us to do for them.
There has not been a tittle of evidence produced to show any change in the conditions prevailing in the United Staltes from May 21, 1929, until to-day. Those remarks were made after the conference had taken place in the city of Ottawa, at which conference the right hon. gentleman's own ministers
Export Act-Mr. Bennett

attended for the purpose of indicating their views with respect to the matter. The magazines of that country have discussed the positions now prevailing, a noteworthy article having appeared in Plain Talk dealing with present day conditions in Michigan. Let us look at another observation made by the hon. minister, as follows:
If clearances would no longer be granted, the result would be that shipments of liquor to the United States would not go from recognized customs ports of the Canadian border and the traffic would be forced under ground to the corruption of Canadian people where perhaps it has not extended to Canada as it has to the United States.
When the right hon. gentleman proposed this measure to the house in the terms in which he did, I asked him if this meant the corruption of the Canadian people last year why it does not mean their corruption now. That is the question. This difference of opinion between the Prime Minister and his colleague, as I said on the second reading of this bill, means the destruction of the foundation upon which responsible institutions rest; the solidarity of the cabinet is the basis of our government. The minister continued:
It seems to me that in that case, if the liquor cannot go out through a recognized customs port in Canada, it will go out through perhaps every little landing place that may exist along our boundaries lined with lakes and rivers.
Our lakes and rivers have not changed. The building of the Beauharnois canal may have been commenced, but the lakes and rivers are still there. Has the hon. gentleman changed the geography of Canada? Did he mean what he said on that occasion? Does he now agree to what the right, hon. the Prime Minister says? An hon. member having interjected the remark "and worse liquor" and the minister continued:
Perhaps worse liquor, and the difficulty from our point of view will be that it will then be illegally exported.
Where is the moral issue? In one case it is illegally exported and in another it is legally exported; which is right? The minister continued :
As the matter stands now, the export of liquor from Canada is absolutely legal.
Let the Prime Minister stand up and condemn his own government or let him rise in his place in this House of Commons and accept the words of a member of his own administration. When the Minister of National Revenue spoke, he spoke for the government-he said distinctly that he was speaking for the government, and he was speaking in the presence of the Prime Minister. Listen to these words:

If we pass a law prohibiting clearance, the liquor will then go out in any case, but it will go out illegally and secretly instead of openly, aboveboard and subject to a certain amount of observation, because we have limited the number of places from which exportation can be made.
Only ten months ago it was legal for the officials of the government to enagage in this business and although the right hon. the Prime Minister says that he does not desire the officials to be engaged in this enterprise, four years passed without a word of condemnation being uttered. The right hon. the Prime Minister permitted his colleague to rise in his place and make the observations to which I have just referred, both in his presence and with his approval. We have listened to deductions as to the high moral attributes of the government in passing this measure, and we have listened to what the right hon. gentleman had to say with respect to the conditions on the international boundary. But the minister continued:
I mentioned this afternoon that when the excise was paid on liquor manufactured in Canada. the liquor became free goods and could be exported the same as any other commodity. I repeat that because I want to add this further observation: that being the case, we cannot stop the exportation of that liquor from any customs port in the Dominion. We have limited the number of docks, but that has not resulted in stopping the exportation of liquor through those ports. We can limit the number of docks within any one port as we did, for example, at Windsor; but we cannot, under the present law, stop the export through any open port in the Dominion. There are those who say-and I have in mind now a prominent Toronto newspaper-that if we passed a law prohibiting the granting of clearances we would at least have washed our national hands of an offence against a friendly neighbour and that, having done that, we would be under no obligation to spend money or time to uphold the laws of the United States. I cannot agree with that, view.
Yet that is the view put to this house by the right hon. the Prime Minister as one of the reasons why we should support this bill. They are not the reasons that I have given which governed our customs committee in 1926, but the reasons now given by the Prime Minister were denounced by his minister ten months ago in these words:
I cannot agree with that view. I cannot escape the conclusion that we then assume a responsibility which now rests upon the United States.
Yesterday, when we were pressing this matter upon the attention of the house, where was the voice of the Minister of National Revenue? Where was he when we were pointing out that the language of this measure meant that Canada assumed a responsibility for the search of ships? He says: "I cannot

Export Act-Mr. Bennett
agree with the view put forward last year by the Toronto newspapers. It means that we must assume a responsibility which now rests upon the United States." He proceeded:
As the matter stands, if there is any violation of law it is a violation of United States law. As it would be under the new law, it would be a violation of Canadian customs law. The law is the law, and we cannot shirk responsibility as readily as that suggestion would make it appear. If a Canadian customs law is violated, surely it becomes the duty of Canadian customs officers to see that that violation is punished. I am not trying to exaggerate; I do not think I am drawing a fanciful picture at all, but I say that if we are under an obligation in the Department of National Revenue to see that violations of the law are punished, surely we shall need to establish a preventive force a good deal larger than the one we have now, which, I may say, is giving me enough trouble as it is. I am sure the most ardent prohibitionist will not say that this country should be under any obligation to spend large sums of money in employing many mtn to see that that law prohibiting the exportation of liquor is not violated. Nations have not yet become quite so altruistic as that.
This is the government speaking.
Besides that, we would not succeed;-
The government then said:

we could not stop the exportation of liquor, although it might be lessened to some extent. After we had passed a law of that kind and liquor still continued to flow into the United States, I feel sure that our neighbours would yet be much inclined to criticise and we would continue to get the blame.
Compare that with the language of yesterday, the language of last week. Compare the language of the government; ten months ago and now. It is Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. The minister goes further and says:
But I will also say very frankly that I am more concerned with stopping smuggling into Canada than stopping smuggling into the United States.
How much has been done by the hon. gentleman since then to give effect to his then conviction? Ten months ago he was concerned over smuggling into Canada and yet the diplomatic correspondence brought down shows that in ten months not a single word has been written to deal with it. Nothing was done till Saturday last when, after we on this side of the house had pointed out that the government was dealing with the question by a jug-handled piece of legislation instead of a reciprocal treat3r, the Prime Minister suddenly became interested and started to negotiate a treaty.

maintopic: EXPORT ACT AMENDMENT

speechtext:
It may have been done at the instance of some of my friends' friends, but the right hon. gentleman has more information on that (point than I have and I have usually observed that he knows a great deal more about other people's business than he does about the business of this country. It would be very desirable if, instead of thinking about other hon. gentlemen's friends' friends, he were thinking about a treaty that might have been negotiated with the United States at any time during the past four years, instead of waiting until the matter was brought up in parliament by the opposition. And then with that sudden conversion that ofbtimes characterizes bis high moral, perfervid convictions making a rush to negotiate another treaty with the United States.
This is the third reading of the measure and on a previous occasion I pointed out to the house what the attitude of the administration has been. Two long years the United States government waited for a reply to their communication offering this country a reciprocal treaty with respect to customs matters and extradition of those who offended against the customs legislation of either country. From 1925 to 1927 they waited. Then there followed a further period of two years until at last a conference was held and now in 1930 the government introduces legislation to do what? To provide against clearances being granted to liquor-laden ships going to the United States, but which legislation the Minister of National Revenue, who still occupies his place in the administration-if he were a self-respecting minister he would have long since resigned -ten months ago said was not capable of success. I say this and I am well within the mark when I refer to the history of Great Britain: when one of the ministers of the British cabinet made known to the public, before the prime minister bad seen it, a letter which was addressed to a government department, the prime minister asked for and was tendered the resignation of his minister.
Export Act-Mr. Bennett

But we have here the picture of a minister who, representing the government of this country, last year made a statement in which he condemned in unmeasured terms the attitude which the same government now takes. He now bows the neck to the Prime Minister and says: You are right; I am always wrong but I wili remain; the people were misled by me a year ago, but they are now being led by my leader. A self-respecting minister would resign and ministers have resigned for less. Take the ease of Mr. Tarte; take the case of other ministers I might mention, who have resigned because of differences o>f opinion on issues not as great as this. The position is quite clear. If the minister was leading the Canadian people along right lines ten months ago, he is wrong now, because there is not on the records of this parliament a single word to justify a change of heart on the part of anyone.
But an election is in sight; a great moral issue was to divert the people's minds from the real issue before the country, and the right hon. gentleman thought with the aid of the editors of the Toronto Star, the Toronto Globe and the Manitoba Free Press, those great pundits, he could divert the people's minds from our critical national condition and on a great moral issue they could retain a little larger place and power.
The people are getting a little weary of that sort of clap-trap. They are beginning to wonder why if, ten months ago, the government decided not to make a reciprocal treaty with the United States now, only ten months later, the Prime Minister should stand up and condemn in unmeasured terms every word uttered by his Minister of National Revenue. How can you have responsible government under conditions like that? How long in Great Britain would a minister of the crown permit himself to be thus publicly insulted' by his prime minister and held up as a joke to the public? What are people hereafter to believe when the Minister of National Revenue rises in his place and says: This is the correct course to pursue. They will say: Let us wait ten months and see what the Prime Minister says; he will repudiate it.
In addition to that we have the statement made yesterday by the Prime Minister of this country that we are now to negotiate a reciprocal treaty with the United States of America. We are to negotiate a treaty that the United States offered to us nearly five years ago, that they asked us to confer about five years ago, and we declined for two years even to answer their despatches. Two years later, as I say, we had a conference and now, instead of introducing legislation after TMr. Bennett.l
a treaty, we are, by force of public opinion passing legislation which will operate against ourselves, according to the Minister of National Revenue, and we are proposing later to negotiate a treaty. We give to the press reports from Washington and our own country that despatches went forward on Saturday last asking for the negotiation of a treaty. Name me any treaty that this government has negotiated that has not been a fiasco. In 1924 they negotiated a treaty with the United States in regard to liquor and smuggling, in which treaty they asked His Majesty the King to say that he was desirous of suppressing smuggling; and the Prime Minister stands in his place in this house and reads the regulations that were adopted by the government to assist in sending intoxicating liquors to the United States, ensuring that such liquor was, in the words of the Minister of National Revenue, being legally shipped to the United States. As the minister said in 1929, it was legal then to do it, although in 1924 we signed a treaty in which the name of His Majesty was used to express a desire to suppress smuggling. Oh, what a spectacle! And now in 1930, on the 24th day of March, the Prime Minister tells us that we are to negotiate a treaty with the United States of America. The old Australian treaty over again, I suppose, when the minister went down there to negotiate and came back with proposals that would have been acceptable to the Canadian people, but abandoned them and was compelled to place a dumping duty on Australian goods for the purpose of doing indirectly that which he could not directly do. The treaty operates just as we indicated it would. The same with New Zealand; France the same, shutting out Canadian wheat while France enjoys all the benefits conferred under the treaty; Italy and other countries the same; and now this government is to negotiate a treaty with the United States for the reciprocal prohibition of imports that are prohibited entrance into the two countries, after we have passed a statute giving the United States what they want. Oh, what a spectacle! Is it any wonder that the people of Canada ask themselves what it all means? Who is sincere, the Minister of National Revenue or the Prime Minister?

I am glad that the Minister of Justice has had a vision. We have not heard from him in this case. I am glad that the Minister of Justice has had a vision because he negotiated the treaty of 1924. His

Export Act-Mr. Lapointe
signature appears on it, and that is the treaty that said: If you have a suspicion that the liquor is going to Mexico in a rowboat, refuse clearance; but if you know that it is going to the United States in a ship grant a clearance. Is it any wonder that, applying the principles of international comity, the United States said: If you admit that you should not clear for the United States indirectly, we ask you in good morals and good faith to say that you will not do it directly. Now we are passing this legislation, instead of a treaty, and we are thereby dispossessing ourselves of the one single weapon we would have in negotiating the treaty namely, to be in a position to say that we will not make a treaty with the United States unless we get a reciprocal arrangement covering all articles smuggled into Canada from the United States. But we are not going to do that. We pass the law first, and make the treaty afterwards.
These, sir, seem to me to be considerations that should weigh mightily in the minds of the members of this house, not in connection with the passage of this legislation, but in asking ourselves why the government has been so derelict in its duty, so changeable in its opinions, so long delayed in taking the action it has. These are questions that we have the right to ask the government. We asked them on the second reading of this bill. We ask them now on the third reading of this bill, now that the amendments have been made which the government thinks are ample for the purpose of guaranteeing this country against the dangers which the Minister of National Revenue foresaw. We on this side can only say, the principle of this bill having, without division, been approved, the amendments having been approved, without division, and the bill now standing for third reading and about to pass, that this country has a right to know whether the Minister of National Revenue meant what he said a year ago and for conditions unchanged-there is no evidence of a change-was he right then or is he right now? We have also a right to ask whether the Prime Minister and his friends around him, who are so ready to accuse us of moral turpitude if we neglect to take steps to pass this legislation-and we have no power to do so- have overlooked the fact that since 1924 he has been as silent as the tomb with respect to this matter that he now considers to be of such pressing and urgent importance. We vote for the third reading, and leave it to the people of this country and the history of Canada to determine whether conduct such as that, so lacking in sincerity, so lacking in conviction upon a great issue, shall long deceive or befog the judgment of the Canadian people.

I cannot resist the
pressing invitation of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and may I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, also to offer a word of comment.
My hon. friend has spoken of the amazing spectacle that he is contemplating at the present time. Let me refer to the still more amazing spectacle that we on this side of the house are witnessing at the present time and have been witnessing since this bill was introduced. We are witnessing the spectacle of hon. gentlemen opposite, under the distinguished leadership of my hon. friend (Mr. Bennett), talking one way and voting the other way. My hon. friend speaks of the solidarity that must exist between members of the government. Surely there must be another solidarity, a solidarity between the vote of a member and his speech.
My hon. friend speaks of Doctor Jekyll and Mr. Hyde. What about the Jekyll who speaks and the Hyde who votes?
My hon. friend also speaks of hypocrisy. He did so the other dlay. I do not want to use such a word, but if my hon. friend is so ardent, so keen, about refusing to grant clearances to liquor vessels, how is it that he did not say a word about it last year? How is it that he did not say a word about it the year before?
My hon. friend the leader of the opposition speaks of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Euler) having spoken last year against this policy, but if I remember well, the refusal to prohibit these clearances was the only-policy which was received with commendation at that time by hon. gentlemen opposite and by their press throughout the country. Even up to the very day this bill was introduced, the whole Conservative press of Canada, at least, the one I read, rvas unanimously-opposed to this policy, and I know well enough the connection of my hon. friend with his press to know that if he had been wilting to go in another direction, his press would have followed him in that direction.
Mr. BF/NNETT: I aim sorry you are mistaken.

public leadership of the Prime Minister of Canada is the spectacle that we have been witnessing in this chamber for the last few days, of hon. gentlemen opposite not daring to oppose this bill, but being afraid to support it fairly and squarely.

Well, some people
either by temperament or by circumstances are in the happy situation of being able to say what they think, others are not.
I wish to attach myself purely and simply to that very important declaration made by the Prime Minister. I will not quarrel with him because perhaps-I do not know-perhaps he might have preceded the introduction of this bill with the declaration he made last night. But taking the declaration as it is, and I so take it, and apprehending that the government is at present negotiating with the United States and will shortly come before this parliament with the draft of a treaty to be ratified, may I in my humble capacity as a member of this house make a couple of friendly suggestions to the government with regard to the conditions that ought to be attached to that treaty, or if you prefer, with regard to the ground that should be covered by it.
I understood the Prime Minister to say- and in this respect he practically agreed with the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), and with my friend from St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Caban)-that the treaty should not only cover the liquor issue but a much broader ground. I welcome this announcement from various points of view; but there are two that I wish especially to bring to the attention of the government and the house this afternoon. The object of this legislation-and, I repeat, I take it to be sincere-is to make for easier cooperation between this country and the United States as regards the violation of the customs laws on both sides. It goes further. We undertake to pass legislation to help the United States in having their own laws observed. I have heard it expressed in this house and outside that it was a shame for the government of Canada to derive profits from a traffic which means the violation of the laws of another country. With that view I aim inclined to agree, but I respectfully submit, Mr. Speaker, that if we want to impress upon the minds of the people of this country that, as an aot of proper neighbourliness, it is proper to force our people to respect the law of another country, we should invite the government of that country to impress the minds of their own people with the duty to respect their own law.

Export Act-Mr. Bourassa
Yesterday, I mentioned casually what had remained in my memory from a hasty reading of a despatch published in the Mail and Empire. I have read it more carefully since, and it is worse than I expected, or rather it reveals a state of things worse than what I described yesterday. The amount of money involved is not as large as what I indicated. The government of the United States is suing a certain person, an American citizen, not for income tax accruing from profits derived from the violation of the laws of the United States, but for a surplus tax. In other words, the government of the United States was already apprised of the fact that that party had been violating the laws of his country for years; the government of the United States had already received hundreds of thousands of dollars in income tax upon profits derived from the importation of liquor against the basic law of the country; the government of the United States was an accomplice and a profiteer in that violation of its own laws, and is now seeking before an American tribunal to make good its claim for a further share of profits derived from that violation.
Therefore I suggest that if we are to have the morality-much has been said about morality in the course of this debate-if we are to have the clear conscience of the people of Canada at the back of this legislation, we should say politely, as language should always be expressed between governments as between gentlemen, to the United States government, that if it wishes the people of Canada to observe the spirit of a law passed in Canada to help the government of the United States in making good its own laws, the American government should do something along the same lines. If it is wrong-and it is wrong- for Canadian citizens to derive profits from the export of liquor to the United States, what do you think of the morality of a government which receives annually millions of dollars in income tax collected from profits derived from violation of the Volstead Act? That condition exists within the knowledge of every public man and public official of the great republic to the south.
A couple of years ago I was talking about this matter with one of our own officials, one of the heads of the income tax branch of the Department of National Revenue. He is a highly informed gentleman. He had been in the United States, and while there, had obtained knowledge of the working of their income tax department; and he told me that it was a matter of course that millions and millions of dollars of the income tax in the United States came from profits derived or 2419-*o
accrued through violation of the Volstead Act. He said that the government of the United States had pledged itself, by the whole force of its law, never to reveal the sources of those profits, provided the bootleggers concerned gave proper returns showing their incomes, and paid their income taxes to the treasury of the American government. The piece of news which appeared in yesterday's Mail and Empire is confirmation of this statement. The suit is taken by the American government for violation of the income tax; it is not for violation of the Volstead Act; but it asks from the millionaire mentioned in the article the surplus tax which he failed to pay because of the profits made in the violation of the Volstead Act, and from which the American government and nation derive a large source of their revenue.
It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, since we are going to work in conjunction with that government in setting up a new standard of morality, we should suggest to them to do their share in the raising of that standard, and especially in putting it into force in their own country.
My second point is this. I learn that in these negotiations the government is going to speak of other "commodities." I think they were called "other goods," by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett); you may give it whatever name you like. They are going to deal with other goods that are the object of smuggling between the two nations. The Prime Minister said yesterday, if I am not mistaken, that there were very few of them at the present time forbidden by our law. There is one, however, which I think is forbidden by our law and which ought to be forbidden by the law of any-shall I say Christian country? It is very difficult to say what countries are Christian these days-a "commodity" the importation of which should be forbidden in any decent country, and that is, obscene literature. Time and again in the house and in private intercourse with the various gentlemen who have occupied the position of Minister of National Revenue I have called attention to the fact that every day, by every train travelling from the United States to Canada, tons of printed paper are brought into this and other cities of the Dominion, scattered throughout our book shops and sold at every book stall and street corner. Thus the worst and most obscene type of literature is laid before our boys and girls coming out of school. If you have observed things in Canada during the last ten years you will have witnessed the frightful increase in juvenile delinquency and criminality. The importation of this type of reading matter is one of the main causes of that degradation.

Export Act-Mr. Eider

la this I am not only expressing the views of the clergy of various religious denominations, but I express the opinions of magistrates in our large cities who preside over juvenile courts. They have told in public and in private that the increase of depravity among the youth of our land is tremendous, and that one of the main causes of it is the enormous amount of obscene literature imported from the United States.
It may be that our chief concern is to prevent the Americans from drinking Canadian whisky, and to force them to drink moonshine whisky made in their own country; but I am more concerned with the moral, mental and physical health of the boys and girls in Canada than I am with the state of souls and bodies of people on the other side of the line. As the father of a family in Canada I respectfully appeal to the leaders of the three parties in this house. I have a family of four boys and three girls whom I am endeavouring to develop into good Canadians and Christians. With that in mind I ask this government to take some means to obtain from the United States a similar measure to the one we have in hand, so that they may do something to keep on their own side of the line the obscene stuff which is imported to this country with the leave of American authorities and, too often, with the complacency of Canadian officials. The late Mr. Boivin, the predecessor of the hon. gentleman who occupies the position of Minister of National Revenue, took some means to put a stop to this importation. The hon. minister wrho occupies that position to-day has also taken action in that direction; but so long as the Americans do not render us the same service of good neighbourliness which we are now undertaking to render to them, all the efforts of my hon. friend will be useless. Just as we are handicapped in the prevention of whisky smuggling, if the American officials are not in earnest in accomplishing their part of the work, likewise, we cannot preserve the morality of the youth of our country unless the Americans will help us. This is the other point I had in mind. I hope that in these negotiations the representatives of Canada will be just as much concerned with the morality of our youth as they are with the soberness, real or affected, of our neighbours.

speechtext: Well, generally speaking, I have not much use for the dumping duty at all.

speechtext:
Well, in view of the
fact that Australian export butter is still bonused, I have no objection to tbp application of the dumping duty under the cir-

cumstamces. When a country starts to bonus its exports, it places itself in a different position altogether from a country which does not bonus its exports.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is that bonus

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE

Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not wish to detain the house for any length of time, but certain criticisms have been levelled against the action taken by the United Farmers of Alberta at their last annual convention, and it is my purpose to deal with those criticisms. The first criticism came from my hon. friend the member for Weyburn (Mr. Young). When the Australian treaty as applied to New Zealand was under discussion in this house he made certain remarks with regard to my position on that treaty. I am not going to read all that he said on the occasion, and anything that I do quote from Hansard, Mr. Speaker, will be on a point of privilege, because I submit the statement then made is not correct. He said he was very much disappointed in the attitude of the members in this corner of the house, particularly myself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That is correct.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
He goes on to talk
about the principles which we have stood for for so long, and he says:
They have here advocated protection for the farmer and asked for the abrogation of this treaty in so far as it applied to New Zealand.
I never made such a statement, Mr. Speaker. It is incorrect. The only reference I made to the Australian treaty in the course of my address early in the session as it applied to New Zealand was, in part, as follows:
and finally concluded a treaty with the Australian government, which treaty was finally extended to New Zealand.
That is the only reference I made to New Zealand at all. I did not discuss the Australian treaty in any shape or form as it was applied to New Zealand. I discussed the Australian treaty primarily on the grounds that I am discussing it this afternoon. My hon. friend evidently is disappointed with members in this comer of the house because of the fact that in annual convention the United Farmers of Alberta passed a certain resolution, and because we had given voice to the wishes of the organization of which we are members. But my hon. friend had better look

Australian Treaty-Mr. Gardiner
to his own methods of procedure first before he criticizes any one else. I have noticed him on many occasions vote against the very principle which he had been criticizing us for not bringing before this house. For instance, last session he had an opportunity of voting for an amendment to the budget which we in this corner of the house moved, extending the principle of the British preference, but he voted against it. That is only one example of my hon. friend's attitude in this house, and certainly he is not in a position to criticize hon. members in this corner as he did when he spoke on the Australian treaty as it applied to New Zealand.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Might I suggest that
that is what the amendment was moved for.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
The amendment was moved for the purpose of giving every member in this house who believed in the extension of the British preference an opportunity to vote for it. If my hon. friend did not discern that, I am sorry both for him and his constituents.
Now, sir, I come to my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown). The hon. member a few days ago startled the house by stating that he was going to discuss what he called the " great apostasy." In order to make sure just exactly what the word means I referred to the dictionary. I found " apostasy " defined as meaning " change in principle." Now, I do not think my hon. friend can ever logically charge us with changing our principles. He devoted a good deal of time to this matter. I am not going to read all that he said, in fact I am not going to read anything of it, because his remarks were not to the point, and had practically no bearing at all on the attitude that we have always taken and the altitude we propose to take on these important matters. But there are one or two points which I must deal with. He called the attention of the house and the country to the fact that the United-Farmers-of-Alberta members were elected on the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture; which is quite true so far as the election of 1921 is concerned. At that time we were elected on that platform because the United Farmers of Alberta in their annual convention the previous year had adopted it. But when the Canadian Council of Agriculture decided to take no further political action, naturally we contended that its platform had to all intents and purposes disappeared. The United Farmers of Alberta took the matter into their own hands, and when that organization in convention passes a resolution on any particular subject which may be a matter of debate in this house, or
a matter which we will have to vote for or against, then we are under the obligation of supporting the attitude of the convention of the United Farmers of Alberta. Our organization is responsible for our platform, and consequently we no longer give allegiance to the platforms of the old Canadian Council of Agriculture. Of course we follow, in its main items, the same line. My hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown), however, seems to think that the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture is something that is going to endure forever. When any member makes such a statement or intimates that it is possible to endure forever it reminds members of this house that under those circumstances we can never expect the hon. member for Lisgar to progress one iota, because of the fact that conditions change. Conditions are always changing, and when we have new conditions we must have new methods of meeting them. The United Farmers of Alberta are alive to this situation, and that is why we to-day adhere to our own platform as enunciated by the annual convention from time to time. Of course, the hon. member's argument would have been much stronger if he himself had adhered to the platform. There have been many occasions in this house when my hon. friend has forgotten the platform of the Canadian Council of Agriculture in order to take care of what might be termed political expediency. We have only to look at the vote taken recently to convince ourselves of that fact, and I might address this question to both my hon. friend from Lisgar and my hon. friend from Weyburn (Mr. Young).
As I stated here, we discussed the Australian treaty 'a few days ago as it applied to New Zealand. An amendment was moved by our Conservative friends, and a suibamendment was moved by a Liberal member of this house. The subamendment had for its purpose the negotiation of a new treaty with New Zealand. I think it is a fair question, in view of the fact that these two hon. members voted for this subamendment, to ask them why they did so. What do they expect to get from a new treaty with New Zealand!? Do they expect, to get more protection and a greater market for the manufacturing interests of this country, or are they hoping that there will be more duties taken off agricultural products?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is it fair to ask the hon.
member why he did not vote?? ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I am not in a position
to say what the attitude of my hon. friends might be, but it is a fair question to ask why

Australian Treaty-Mr. Evans
they voted for the negotiation of a new treaty if according to their own statements, t'he present treaty is doing no harm to this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: May I ask the hon. members why they did not vote at all?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Yes. We did not vote because we are going to vote for the amendment which I shall move a little later. I do not think I shall take the time of the house any longer. We merely desire to bring the matter before the house fairly and squarely, because we are not as satisfied as we should be with the manner in which this treaty was negotiated. As a consequence, it is our wish to have it brought before the house and a vote taken upon it. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I move, seconded by Mr. Evans (Roseitown), the following amendment:
That all the words after the word "that" be struck out and the following words substituted therefor, "in the opinion of this house the present Australian treaty should be abrogated."

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Mr. Evans is the seconder, and I believe he should have the floor.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the discussion that has taken place on the Australian treaty, I feel there are certain truths left unsaid which ought to be brought out.
This treaty, like all others, is designed to give advantage to one class at the expense of another. Trade treaties are as much a part of the plan of privilege as the tariff schedule itself. They are a product of countries in which the chief feature of industry is tariff protection and whose legislation* and commerce are based on legislated privileges. The result of the Australian treaty has been to put a burden on all except those who are in a regular way the beneficiaries of tariff protection. Such treaties have no meaning in a protected country unless the interests of some parties are sacrificed for the benefit of others. There may be exceptions to this, of course. Let us suppose that Australia had something which Canada had not, or vice versa. For instance, if Canada and Australia exchanged nickel for raisins, in a free way, it would be beneficial to both, but treaties are not made that way in a protected country. To call particular attention to that fact I want this house to witness the raisin manipulation of the Australian treaty. Our government and the government of Australia knew that Australia was unable to supply Canada with 
raisins. Why the government increased the duty on raisins from all countries except Australia is known only to themselves; we are just left here to guess. It is certainly a part of the Australian treaty which cannot be defended on any business principle, and can only be described as a callous act of injustice perpetrated on the consuming public of Canada It shows an utter disregard for the rights of the workers, including the farmers. I repeat, we can only guess at the reason, because trade treaties are not made on the plan of the one with Australia except so far as a bargain is possible between the politician and the prospective beneficiaries. I was very much amused to hear the hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) Lecture the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Irvine) in the supposition that the hon*. member for Wetaskiwin was advocating protection on eggs. Well, there the hon. member for Lisgar stands, defending his party which trades off the right of one class for the benefit of another. I say that the Australian* treaty should be abrogated, if for no other reason than the manipulation of the tariff -on raisins. Surely it is indefensible from every point of view to add a million and a half dollars to the cost of living of the workers of this country. I want to say, and I say it deliberately, that the Australian treaty was created on an uneconomic foundation. It is not only uneconomic, Mr. Speaker,
I say it is immoral.
A good many times during the last few months the question has been asked why the farmers are opposed to this treaty, and why they have turned to -protection. The farmers are not protectionists; if they had protection it would be futile to expect any benefit therefrom because it is all passed on in enhanced prices until it comes down to the man on the land, who has no means of making the other fellow pay. His products are always sold at world's prices. The duty on butter before the Australian treaty came into operation gave the farmer no advantage, even though most of the butter at that time was made by the farmers. The duty never gave the farmer a price-fixing power, which is the purpose of the tariff on all other commodities. When the time came to make a treaty with Australia and New Zealand, the farmers were absolutely forgotten.
The Australian treaty was extended to New Zealand by order in council. New Zealand is a country which had nothing to export but the very things for which the farmers of Canada were trying to find a profitable market. The government put through the deal by order in council; as far as the people of Canada

Australian Treaty-Mr. Evans
were concerned this extension to the treaty was carried out in a secret manner, but I want to strip from this discussion with regard to the Australian treaty the smoke screen from behind which both parties have been trying to snipe at the farmers and get them to ask for protection. I am not blaming the Australian treaty altogether for the condition in which the agriculturists of this country find themselves to-day; that it has been unjust to agriculture goes without saying, but I blame the Liberal party for its callousness in raising the cost of living and increasing the cost of production to our farmers. At the same time I blame the Conservative party for capitalizing the present state of agriculture and seizing on the New Zealand part of the Australian treaty to confuse our farmers, while neither the Conservatives nor the Liberals care one whit for agriculture. They have taken this action to confuse our people into asking for a protective measure which will be to their disadvantage.
I hold in my hand a letter from a friend of mine whom I have never seen, which I desire to read in order to clarify the situation. He says:
I duly received your letter of March 1st, and I am glad I did not answer it before as I now send you a clipping from yesterday's Toronto Star which will go to show you the big business that would profit by a 4 cents duty on New Zealand butter. If, as I read recently, the Canadian market is the highest priced market for butter in the world, with such a price that butter shipped from New Zealand to England can be profitably reshipped to Canada and, at added steamship and rail transportation charges be profitably sold in Ontario towns, it does not look as if the dairy interests of Canada were suffering. It is the big interests, such as this proposed merger or its intended component parts, that would principally profit by the 4 cent import duty, and the consumer would pay that and more for his butter and would be more firmly in the grasp of the hand of the producing monopoly.
I am not and never was a farmer, but have always contended the farmer was the worst paid man on the job. Let me ask you to get the Atlantic Monthly for March and read "A Dirt Farmer Speaks His Mind." I feel the same way as the dirt farmer.
That is signed by George E. Davis, of Broekville.
This is really the first time in the history of Canadian agriculture that the political parties in this house have advocated protection on an agricultural product, and which apparently would give the farmer a price fixing power, but we should tear off the mask of hypocrisy which covers this whole question. Let the farmers see the grinning monster which is behind this demand for protection on butter at the present time. Let it be understood that the Canadian farmer is not the one who is asking for this protection; it is being asked for by some of the same gentlemen who profited on the anguish of this nation during the war. They are again directing the raid on the rights of the consumers, and in all probability are getting ready for the next war. Let me read a clipping from the Toronto Star of March 17 of this year:
A chain of dairies having one control and stretching across Canada was brought one step nearer completion when the Dairy Corporation of Canada, by a $S50,000 deal bought control of two dairy product companies in Regina and Winnipeg. It is expected that one or more of the Ontario dairies will also be absorbed by the corporation.
Then I should like to read another clipping from the same paper under date of March 10, of this year:
A creamery merger in Ontario of plants worth approximately $2,500,000, engineered by English capital, is expected to be announced by cable to-day	The largest creamery concerned is to be Flavelle's Limited at Lindsay. Some fifty of the two hundred plants in Ontario are concerned in the move which aims at cheaper operation and greater production, with more centralized control. The plants extend from Carleton Place in the east to Petrolea in the west.
It is learned to-day on good authority that five large English financial houses are to be partners in the merger. One of the shareholders already has a large stake in the dairy business of Lovell and Christmas, at Montreal, one of the best known houses in Canada. Another of the English firms behind the Ontario creamery merger is the Maypole firm, which runs one of the largest chain store businesses in the world.
Here is the cream of the whole thing: Consequent to the creamery merger will in all probability be a movement for raising the duty on New' Zealand butter, now one cent a pound.
The sum total of these things is the demand for a duty to be placed on butter. The Liberal party consummated the Australian treaty about the same time as the Liberal partv in Saskatchewan was manipulating the cooperative creamery concerns in that province in such a way as to bring them under private control. The thing is growing and will grow until there is to be one great merger stretching across the country which will be a manufacturing business with the high protection given to everything else. I hope the people of Saskatchewan soon will see through this creamery muddle, that they will not be caught in the round-up which is being engineered by the protectionists of this Dominion who are trying to bring together the several lines of agriculture and have them demand protection. The farmer is not asking for protection.

Australian Treaty-Mr. Evans
Both parties know that Canada is an agricultural country and it would be a terrible thing for the privileged clients of both parties if it were not. They both speak of the value of the home market and have carried on that joke for thirty years, but I do not think the farmers believe it. For thirty years both parties have carried on a vigorous immigration policy while every possible burden has been placed on the agriculturist. They do not care how many will be forced off the land, so long as they can fill our places with immigrants from central Europe who are willing to accept a lower standard of living. The farmer is being asked to bear the expense of bringing out these immigrants who will take his place upon the land. The farmer is being driven out of business by the rising cost of production and-

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Does the hon. member suggest that we deport all immigrants?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: You can do with them as you will. This Australian treaty intensifies these conditions. The country must decide which of two policies it will pursue. The settlement of the land will not be permanent without complete freedom of exchange.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Is that the
reason the hon. member desires to raise the tariff?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member has put the cart before the horse.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: You mean the cart before the mule.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: We demand complete freedom of exchange. This government is bartering away the rights of the farmers in order to give the tariff-fed manufacturers freer entry for their goods into the Australian market. That country has been corrupted by the same system of trade penalties and the rights of one class are being sacrificed for the advantage of another. That is why the treaty was consummated so easily, for that country has been burdened with the same system of privilege as has Canada. Since the last election the Conservative party has been endeavouring to round up those engaged in the different branches of agriculture.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Including yourself.	j j * j

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
From what has appeared in
the newspapers of both parties as well as from what has been said in different speeches delivered throughout the country, it seems that they are trying to confuse the farmer into asking for protection, the cattle raisers, the onion growers, the sugar beet growers, the bean growers, and the egg and poultry producers 
are being invited by the protectionist press to ask for protection. Is it any wonder that many farmers have been misled. Let me tell my protectionist friends, and particularly those of the Tory party that it is a mistake for them to pose as the friend of the farmer. They have asked this government to lop off the New Zealand appendage to the Australian treaty but defends the treaty in its original form in order to cum' favour with the manufacturers of automobiles pulp and paper, agricultural implements and other articles. Those manufacturers would be protected by the preservation of the treaty, but let it be understood that we do not want protection. If Canada desires to encourage the flow of population towards the farm, it must abandon this un-economic and unmoral practice of subsidizing the manufacturers at the expense of the farmers. This Australian treaty is a violation of business principles and business ethics. It is part of a scheme to enslave our farmers. Both parties are asking the farmers to vote for a measure which will work to their detriment.
The unemployment situation and the -marketing of wheat are subjects which hinge uipon the uneconomic practice of tying agriculturists to a class which is yearly taking away that freedom which they must have in order to carry on. The -farmers of this country will not long wear the shackles which restrict freedom of exchange, they will not l-ong consent to their rights being bartered away for the benefit of the industrial and capitalistic classes. The Australian treaty will have to go because there is not one reason which can be offered for its retention as a national trade measure. Even th; Minister of Finance could find the other day no stronger defence than the old wornout maxim: We must trade within the empire.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Not worn out.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: Yes, worn out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: I do not agree; I think it is an excellent maxim.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: It is all right, as I said before, if Canada has something to trade in a free way with another country, but the farmers will not longer stand for their interests being bartered away for the sake of some other class.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: The hon. member, then, does not agree with the British preference?

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
What have we to say as regards the paper industry for which the treaty itself seems to exist? We subsidized a line of boats -with the Canadian workers' earnings to find sale for the paper products of our forests, products our own. publishers are starv-

Australian Treaty-Mr. Evans
ing for at prices which are equitable. We are aiding the export to the orient of automobiles, things which cannot be made and sold in Canada unless the government gives the manufacturers the legal right to rob the home consumer of about one-third of the price. Is this reasonable? It seems that all industry depends upon agriculture in this country. I have heard from beginning to end of this session and every session I have been in the house until now. a wail from the protectionists. They cannot stand on their own feet. They have to charge the home consumer a price that gives them a profit over the whole of their output whether it is sold at home or abroad. This cannot continue any longer. I wonder how long the farmers of Canada will allow the government to provide our competitors with agricultural implements at prices cheaper than we can buy them for at home? Canadian-made implements are sold in foreign countries to our own competitors cheaper than the Canadian farmer can buy them.
Even some members of parliament are willing to laugh at the farmers and say that they are becoming protectionists. I should like to know whether the skyscrapers of Toronto and the tariff-built cities of eastern Canada are of more importance to this country than the whole agricultural industry of the Dominion. Why do we maintain on our statute books today an act that makes it possible to plunder the only industry that is worth while, the only one that can stand on its own feet, while our manufacturers fail to learn the simple lesson of economy and morality? I want for the Australian treaty some reason based on equity and justice for all classes. Is it for the good of Canada or not? Is it to be based on mere silly sentimental loyalty of trading *within the empire? If I want to judge the love of the government for other members of the empire, I can point to the restrictions which they have placed upon the British preference.
The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said the other day that we import
50,000,000 pounds of butter per annum. Why do we do that? It is strange, is it not? The reason is simply this: our farmers find it more profitable to do other work than to make butter or perhaps I should put it in another way and say: There is less loss in other things than in making butter. Let me ask the government to-day: if they want us to make butter, why penalize us by an import duty as high as nearly one-third of the value of everything we have to use? I repeat: We are the class that do not ask favours. If my Conservative friends want an explanation as
to why we should have free trade, let them ask their former leader, the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie), when as leader of their party he insisted on free trade in hatbands and hat-sweats.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext: That was because the heads of the government were growing so fast.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Why did the hon. member
for South Wellington insist on this? Perhaps the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) will answer the question. Why all this concern about butter when, if a duty were placed on hatbands, we might have a flourishing industry in that line? There is only one answer: it is not profitable for our hatmakers to make their own hatbands and hat-sweats. If our farmers choose to do something other than to make butter, who should care? But the two-facedness of the whole matter is seen in that our protectionist friends on both sides maintain a duty on all our needs. If you want to help the farmer, give him his necessaries of life free; keep down his cost of production; let him have a chance to do his dairying without being penalized on everything he needs to buy. On churns he is penalized 30 per cent; on cans, moulds, rollers, butter workers, besides all the necessaries of life he is penalized around one-third of the value. Even the salt is charged at a high duty except for those few, such as packers and so on, with whom the politicians can make a bargain. Then, as if it were not enough to charge a duty on salt, the old bags and barrels in which it may be imported pay a duty of 25 per cent as well, although they are things which cannot enter into competition with any Canadian industry.
Two splendid speeches came from the other side of the house when this matter was under discussion on a previous occasion. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Malcolm) and the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn) were both carried away by their eloquence in making excuses for the Australian and New Zealand treaties, but not one reason was given by either of them to show why an added load should be placed on agriculture and labour for the sake of those who already have a licence to plunder these classes. Hon. Ernest Lapointe made a strong appeal in Quebec last Friday night for Canadian unity. There are signs that influences against national unity. are busy. speechtext: The house resumed from March 18 consideration of the motion of Mr. Woodsworth for the second reading of Bill No. 20 to provide in the province of Ontario for the dissolution and the annulment of marriage, and the amendment thereto of Mr. McMillan.

maintopic: SUPPLY-AUSTRALIAN TREATY AMENDMENT TO MOTION OF MINISTER OF FINANCE FOR COMMITTEE
subtopic: DIVORCE COURT FOR ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as one of the members from the province of Ontario, which province is particularly affected by this measure, I wish to give the reasons why I have opposed the bill up to the present time, and why I purpose to continue to oppose it. Among the powers conferred on this parliament by the British North America Act, are those relating to divorce. I presume that everyone will agree with me that those powers should be exercised in such a wise and careful manner as to protect not merely the interests of the parties particularly concerned, but the sanctity and purity of the marital relations and the home.
In the exercise of those powers we have year by year granted to those applying for separation dissolution of the union, with the right to marry again if either sees fit during the lifetime of the other. This dissolution of marriage, I would point out, has always been

Divorce Court jor Ontario
granted by way of privilege and not as a matter of right. Now, however, we are asked by this bill to give to a court in Ontario these powers which parliament possesses. The effect of this bill, if enacted, would be to endow such a court with full powers of divorce. For the first time we are laying down a definite principle on which the proposed divorce court in Ontario would act. We have never before laid down the principle that any husband or wife can come to this parliament or to a court and ask for divorce as a matter of right;
I repeat, parliament has always granted divorce as a matter of privilege. I think we ought to proceed very cautiously before deciding definitely to adopt this principle, which would be applicable not merely to Ontario, but, in, effect, to the whole Dominion.
I know divorce has been a disagreeable matter to us, we in this house have all been "fed-up" with divorce bills, but I do not think we should consider this bill from the standpoint of getting rid of something that is disagreeable to us; rather we should consider it from the standpoint of whether we want to adopt the principle which I have pointed out.
I have no objection to divorce being dealt with through the medium of a court; it might in fact be desirable to do so, because such a court in Ontario could deal wiith other important matters related to divorce, such as the disposition of the children, the granting of alimony, the distribution of the estate and so on. Considered from that point of view it might be convenient to erect a divorce court for Ontario, but I do object to this parliament taking that step now without further consideration.
It is to be noted that if we pass this bill divorce, so far as Ontario is concerned, is practically settled for all time to come, for we can quite understand that if any member in the future should propose that this matter be reconsidered, he would be met with the objection:	We have had this matter up
before, we disposed of it then, and we decline to reconsider it now.
I take the position that it is not necessary to grant absolute divorce in any case. As I have said, we grant divorce now entirely as a matter of privilege. If we are to establish a divorce court in Ontario, why not limit its power to granting a decree of separation only, without the right to marry again, and see how far that will go in dealing with this divorce evil. It may be that many applicants for divorce will be satisfied with such a separation without the right of remarriage. I think we should try that experiment before adopting this bill.
The question naturally arises, are the people from Ontario asking for this measure? I question very much whether they want a divorce court established in their province, that is, a court with power to grant absolute relief from marital responsibilities. I think there should be some further investigation made to find out what the people of Ontario really want before this bill is enacted. For instance, what does the provincial government wish; has it expressed any opinion in regard to the establishment of a divorce court in the province? I think not. Then, has this government considered the matter carefully? It is an important matter and we should have from the government some expression of opinion as to the wisdom of passing this proposed Legislation.
For these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I am not in favour of the bill at the present time, and I intend to oppose it as far as I am able.

speechtext:
(Prime Minister):	Mr. Speaker, as I was
absent on the previous occasions on which this subject was discussed in the house, I feel I should like, before casting my vote this evening, to state my position in reference to this bill.
May I say that on the first occasion I was absent intentionally? Perhaps I am assuming too much to imagine that anything I might say would influence any hon. member, but at any rate I thought for many reasons it was advisable that the house should give a free expression of its views without being influenced one way or another by any word of mine. On the second occasion I had an engagement which unfortunately prevented me from being present in the house. However, this evening I am speaking-as is every other member-in my capacity as a private member on a bill which is not a government measure, but a measure which has been introduced by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) as a private member of this house.
It will, I believe, assist us in seeing the whole question' in its proper .perspective if we keep in mind the circumstances under which this bill came to be introduced into this house. This is the same measure, or a measure in similar terms to one which on three previous occasions passed the other house and whioh on one occasion1 previous to this year was introduced in this house but was defeated on second reading. During the course' of the discussion on the bill in this house the discussion changed in large part from the consideration of the matter as one of procedure in reference to the business of
Divorce Court for Ontario

parliament, which was how it was viewed at the outset, to a consideration of the best method of dealing with divorce. There has been considerable confusion in the minds of hon. members as a consequence of that change of emphasis, or possibly subject, if I imay so describe the situation which has arisen. To my mind, it is important that we should see very clearly that our concern in this particular measure is, if I may so express it, a dual one. It has to do, in part, with the procedure of business in this house, and in part with procedure in matters of divorce. There is no question of principle to be discussed, considered or debated in any way; the question of the principle involved in the dealing by this parliament or the courts with divorce was settled many years ago. That principle has been aocepted in this house, and therefore >in the present instance we are not concerned with that phase of the matter at all. What we are very much concerned with, however, is the procedure to be adapted as respecting the granting of divorces in its relation to the business of parliament.
May I say a word as to the procedure in its relation to the business of this parliament? In the first instance, the bill was introduced in the other house because hon. members of the Senate found that their duties as legislators were being materially impeded by the amount of time which it became necessary for them to give ito the various petitions for divorce laid before them for consideration. When the number of petitions was few, the question did not arise; but once the applications for divorce passed the one hundred mark, reached the two hundred mark and eventually the three hundred mark as is the -case to-day, it became a very important matter to hon. members of the other house, and to this house, as to how much of their time might properly be given to the consideration of private measures to the exclusion, in some part, of the time which they rightly felt they should be devoting to public measures.
There is a very important difference in the function of parliament as it deals with private legislation and public legislation. The primary concern of parliament is the consideration of public legislation; that is its business, and it is n-ot primarily concerned with legislation of a private nature. The rules of both houses of parliament make that abundantly clear. There is an entirely different method adopted in respect to private legislation. Those who wish to introduce bills have to proceed by petition in the first instance; those petitions have to be carefully examined, money has to be paid to insure the respective measures re-
ceiving consideration, and parliament in dealing with private legislation acts rather in its judicial than in its legislative capacity. Certainly in regard to this question of divorce parliament is acting primarily as a court, and it is as a court that hon. members consider the several applications for divorce and give to them their time and attention, So long is the judicial side of the duties of members of parliament does not interfere with the legislative side of their duties, I can see no reason- why petitions could not be received in a limited number and dealt with by parliament. It is perfectly clear, however, that if a stage is reached -where private legislation assumes such proportions that as a consequence public legislation has to be neglected or suffer, some other method must be found to deal with matters of private legislation, or they must be left altogether alone. That,
I take it, is how the measure came to this house from the Senate, after having been passed, as I have said, in that house on three previous occasions.
When the bill was introduced last year by my -hon. friend he drew attention very properly to the other factor which I have mentioned, namely, the resultant effects as far as divorce is concerned of the hasty procedure which becomes essential where a very large number rather than a few petitions have to be dealt with. He pointed out that where the other house was concerned with a few petitions members could meet to consider them with care. They could surround each case with the safeguards with which, as a judicial body, they would be expected to surround them! They -could in that way insure the carrying out of a judicial function in a judicial manner. But he pointed out further that where the number had reached, as it had, two or three hundred, it had become necessary for members of the other chamber to form themselves info several! committees in order to cope with the number of divorce cases to be considered. He said that what very frequently happened was that many members were absent from at least part of the proceedings. In some cases I believe it is true that members who had not heard any of the evidence were present at the time of giving a decision and cast their vote. My hon. friend pointed out that that sort of thing was not right, and I agree with him. I do not see how it can be defended. I do not see how one can defend a course of procedure which deals in a haphazard fashion with a great question that affects so vitally the interests not only of individuals but of the family and, to a verv considerable extent of the state

Divorce Court for Ontario
Take the position with regard to the consideration of divorce as it is carried on in this parliament at the present time. The members of the committee are not necessarily members of the legal profession; in fact, large numbers of them are laymen. They are however sitting as judges, and they are performing a judicial function. In the performance of this function it is reasonable to believe that they should follow to some extent and be familiar with the rules and laws of evidence. Gentlemen who are not familiar with those rules and laws cannot possibly be expected to give to that aspect of the situation the care which would be given to it by those who are trained in the law and who have knowledge of the rules governing court procedure. All these questions of divorce involve in large part- matters of law; important questions that have to be considered are legal questions. It might be said with truth that in acting on these questions of divorce this parliament is practically the only court in the world of any considerable importance which is not composed of persons who are trained in the law and which gives its decisions regardless altogether of the rules of evidence which in all other branches of litigation have been found so essential to the protection of society and the rights of individuals.
I think my hon. friend has made out a very strong case as to why some procedure should be adopted different from that which until a few years ago worked very well, but which certainly has not worked well during the last couple of years. I think he proved conclusively, and I think hon. members of both houses will agree, that the present procedure does not sufficiently safeguard the granting of divorces but that, if anything, it makes the obtaining of divorce much easier than it has been at any previous time. Everyone knows with respect to petitions for divorce that there is a great deal of lobbying; members are persuaded to be present at a hearing or to be absent; sometimes one group will be present to hear part of a case discussed and another group will be present to hear another part discussed. In a great number of cases, at least, all of the members have not heard all of the evidence, and as a result many petitions are granted which perhaps would not be granted were a strict judicial procedure followed.
In addition, as my hon. friend has pointed out, this parliament can give no consideration to questions of alimony and can make no direction with regard to children who may be affected by the decree. These are both factors which are all-important and which, it
seems to me, very properly come within the scope of provincial jurisdiction, the provinces being charged, among other things, with matters affecting civil rights. The point I wish to stress at the moment is that I believe the case has been made out very clearly and emphatically showing the need of a procedure different from that at present existing being adopted if the number of divorces granted is not to increase rather than decrease. It has been demonstrated that there is a need for something more in the way of proper safeguards, something in the way of procedure along judicial lines, whether that procedure is to be adopted by this parliament or by some other body. The other point, which I think has been equally strongly presented and made out, is the necessity, as far as this parliament is concerned, of our finding some other procedure in dealing with these numerous petitions in order to save the time of parliament for public business, rather than having so much of it consumed in a consideration of private legislation.
That, I think, broadly is a correct and accurate statement of the situation. I hope hon. members of the house, and people throughout the country generally, will appreciate that all we are discussing and considering in this matter at the present time is the question of procedure. That is a point which I think cannot be too strongly emphasized. We are considering a question of procedure, procedure which must be revised in the interests of the prevention of the increase of divorces, and equally in the interests of this parliament proceeding with its proper and legitimate business.
My hon. friend from South Huron (Mr. McMillan) has moved an amendment to the bill which is before the house. If my hon. friend's amendment carries, the bill will be defeated. That will mean that we will be back in ithe position we occupied at the end of last session and during the beginning of this session. We will not have solved the question of procedure one way or the other; we will still have to find some means of dealing with this question, and we will have to find it immediately unless more and more of our time during this session is to be devoted to the consideration of these divorce bills rather than to the great (public measures which are our real concern. I may say with regard to my hon. friend's amendment that it seems to me to express a very obvious and desirable object. I find it very hard, as I think every hon. member of the house will find it hard, to disagree with what my hon. friend says; in fact I think he has given expression to what
